book.description: Data and sampling, events and distributions, random variables, joint models, sampling limits, estimation, testing, regression, and Bayesian updating. Every lesson includes derivations, worked examples, exercise solutions, and local interactive demonstrations.
book.audience: Learners with elementary algebra; continuous probability requires single-variable integration, and joint densities use basic double integrals.
book.scope: A complete introductory course in ten chapters and fifty lessons. The first half develops probability and sampling models; the second develops frequentist inference, basic linear models, and Beta–binomial Bayesian inference. Measure-theoretic probability, advanced stochastic processes, multiple regression, comprehensive experimental design, and advanced nonparametric methods belong to later courses.

reviews.title: Where Data Come From · Chapter Review

questions.problem: Two regions contain $0.7,0.3$ of the population and have means $20,40$. Find the population's weighted mean. Why is it not simply thirty?
questions.hint: The number of samples or groups does not determine their population weights.
solution: A simple average implicitly gives each region half the population weight.
questions.answer: $26$; a simple average uses the wrong population composition.

questions.problem: Volunteers are randomly assigned to treatment and control groups. What conclusions does this support, and what does it not guarantee?
questions.hint: Distinguish recruitment from treatment assignment.
solution: Under the stated experimental conditions, random assignment supports a causal comparison within the sample.
Voluntary participation does not automatically make the sample representative of the target population.
questions.answer: It supports treatment comparisons within the experimental setting, without automatically justifying generalization to the population.

questions.problem: Two events have probabilities $0.5,0.4$ and intersection probability $0.2$. Find their union probability and $P(A\mid B)$, and determine whether they are independent.
questions.hint: Apply the addition rule, conditional probability, and the product criterion separately.
solution: The union probability is $0.5+0.4-0.2=0.7$.
The conditional probability is $0.2/0.4=0.5$, and the intersection equals the product of the marginal probabilities.
questions.answer: Union probability $0.7$; conditional probability $0.5$; the events are independent.

questions.problem: Choose three representatives from eight people, with no distinct roles, then appoint one representative as spokesperson. How many outcomes are possible?
questions.hint: Choose the group, then assign the role.
solution: There are $\binom83=56$ representative groups.
Each group has three possible spokespersons.

reviews.title: Random Variables and Average Behavior · Chapter Review

questions.problem: $X$ equals zero with probability $0.25$ and four with probability $0.75$. Find its expectation and variance.
questions.hint: Calculate the first and second moments.
solution: The variance is $12-9=3$.

questions.problem: Source A accounts for twenty percent of cases and produces an observation with probability $0.6$; source B accounts for eighty percent and produces it with probability $0.1$. After observing it, what is the probability the source was A?
questions.hint: The numerator is the A pathway; the total observation probability includes both pathways.
solution: The pathway probabilities are $0.12,0.08$.
The posterior probability is $0.12/0.2=0.6$.

questions.problem: Three of ten objects are targets. Draw four without replacement. Find the expected target count and the probability of exactly one target.
questions.hint: Use a hypergeometric model; the draws are not independent.
solution: The expectation is $4(3/10)=1.2$.
The probability is $\binom31\binom73/\binom{10}4=105/210$.

questions.problem: A Poisson process averages $0.5$ events per minute and has independent, stationary increments. What is the probability of at least one event in three minutes?
questions.hint: Find the three-minute parameter, then take the complement of zero events.
solution: The three-minute mean is $1.5$.
The probability of zero events is $e^{-1.5}$.

questions.problem: A density is $f(x)=3x^2$ on $[0,1]$. Find its cumulative distribution function and expectation.
questions.hint: Keep the support when integrating.
solution: Within the interval, the cumulative probability is $x^3$; it is zero to the left and one to the right.
The expectation is $\int_0^1 3x^3dx=3/4$.

questions.hint: Standardize both endpoints.
solution: The standard deviation is three, so the endpoints become minus one and one.
The probability is $\Phi(1)-\Phi(-1)$.

questions.problem: Two equally weighted groups have means one and five and within-group variances two. Find the overall mean and variance.
questions.hint: Use total expectation and total variance.
solution: The overall mean is three.
The variance of the group means is four; add the average within-group variance of two.

questions.problem: Two variables have standard deviations one and two and correlation $-0.5$. Find the variance of their sum.
questions.hint: First recover the covariance.
solution: The covariance is minus one.
The variance of the sum is $1+4-2=3$.

reviews.title: From Populations to Samples · Chapter Review

questions.problem: Take sixty-four independent observations from a population with mean six and standard deviation eight. What is the standard error of the mean? If the CLT approximation applies, what is the approximate probability that the mean exceeds eight?
questions.hint: Use the distribution of the sample mean, not the distribution of individual observations.
solution: The standard error is one.
The standardized threshold is two.

questions.problem: An original sample has five records. An ordinary bootstrap uses four hundred repetitions. How many resamples are generated, and how many records are in each? Does this guarantee correction of representativeness bias?
questions.hint: Distinguish the original sample size from the number of repetitions.
solution: Four hundred resamples are generated, each containing five records drawn with replacement.
Resampling still uses the original empirical distribution; selection bias does not automatically disappear.
questions.answer: Four hundred resamples of five records each; correction of bias is not guaranteed.

reviews.title: Estimation and Confidence Intervals · Chapter Review

questions.problem: A normal population has known standard deviation four. A sample of sixty-four has mean ten. Using critical value $1.96$, calculate and interpret a confidence interval for the mean.
questions.hint: Calculate the standard error, then explain repeated-sampling coverage.
solution: The standard error is $4/8=0.5$ and the margin of error is $0.98$.
Under the model, this interval procedure has approximately $95\%$ coverage.
questions.answer: Approximately $[9.02,10.98]$; this is not a posterior probability assigned directly to a fixed parameter.

questions.problem: Twelve paired before-and-after differences have sample mean two and sample standard deviation three. Find the standard error and degrees of freedom for a paired interval.
questions.hint: The number of independent pairs is the sample size.
solution: The standard error is $3/\sqrt{12}$.
The degrees of freedom are eleven.
questions.answer: Standard error approximately $0.8660$; degrees of freedom $11$.

reviews.title: Hypothesis Testing and Decisions · Chapter Review

questions.problem: The null hypothesis is a fair coin, and all five tosses are heads. What is the $p$-value for a prespecified right-sided exact test? What is the decision at $0.05$?
questions.hint: The extreme right tail consists only of all heads.
solution: The probability is $1/32=0.03125$.
It is below the prespecified threshold.
questions.answer: Reject the fairness hypothesis; this does not give it posterior probability $0.03125$.

questions.problem: Five tests are performed together. To control the family-wise error rate at $0.01$, what Bonferroni threshold should each use? Must the tests be independent?
questions.hint: Use the union bound.
solution: Each threshold is $0.01/5=0.002$.
The union bound holds under arbitrary dependence.
questions.answer: Use $0.002$ per test; independence is not required.

reviews.title: Relationships, Models, and Updating · Chapter Review

questions.problem: Least-squares summaries are $n=10,\bar x=2,\bar y=5,S_{xx}=8,S_{xy}=12,\mathrm{SSE}=16$. Find the fitted line and the standard error of its slope.
questions.hint: Fit the line, then estimate the error variance using the residual degrees of freedom.
solution: The slope is $1.5$ and the intercept is two.
The estimated error variance is $16/8=2$ and the slope standard error is $\sqrt{2/8}=0.5$.

questions.problem: The prior is $\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)$, and five of eight trials succeed. Find the posterior and predictive success probability, and state one model assumption.
questions.hint: Add the numbers of successes and failures to the prior parameters.
solution: The posterior is $\operatorname{Beta}(7,5)$.
The predictive probability is $7/12$. The model assumes independent Bernoulli trials with a fixed success probability, among other conditions.

exam.problem: A voluntary online survey finds that users of a tool are more productive. A report claims, “The tool increases everyone's productivity.” Identify at least two unsupported inferential steps.
exam.hint: Examine sampling, treatment assignment, and measurement.
solution: A voluntary sample may suffer from coverage and selection bias.
Tool use was not randomly assigned; confounding or reverse causation may explain the association.
The definition and measurement of productivity must also be clear.
exam.answer: The evidence does not adequately establish causation or generalization to the whole population.

exam.problem: Two independent fair dice are rolled. Given that their sum is seven, what is the probability that the first die is six?
exam.hint: List the ordered outcomes in the conditioning event.
solution: Six equally likely ordered outcomes have sum seven.
Only $(6,1)$ meets the target condition.

exam.problem: Thirty percent of a thousand items come from source A. Defect rates are $0.01$ for A and $0.04$ for B. Given a defective item, what is the posterior probability that it came from A?
exam.hint: Use pathway proportions; there is no need to draw all thousand items.
solution: The defective-item pathway probabilities are $0.003$ for A and $0.028$ for B.
The denominator is $0.031$.

exam.problem: Independent repeated trials have success probability $0.2$. Find the probability of exactly one success in the first five trials and the expected total number of trials until the first success.
exam.hint: A fixed number of trials and a fixed success target require different models.
solution: The binomial probability is $\binom51(0.2)(0.8)^4=0.4096$.
The expected geometric waiting time is $1/0.2=5$.

exam.problem: A joint density equals two on $0<x<y<1$. Find $f_X(x)$ and $E[Y\mid X=x]$, and determine whether the variables are independent.
exam.hint: Integrate over the other coordinate, then normalize.
solution: Conditionally, $Y$ is uniform on $(x,1)$, with mean $(x+1)/2$.
The conditional distribution changes with $x$, so the variables are not independent.

exam.problem: An independent sample comes from a population with standard deviation twelve. The current sample size is thirty-six. What sample size would reduce the standard error of the mean from two to one? Would this automatically remove selection bias?
exam.hint: Distinguish square-root gains in precision from sample representativeness.
solution: Solving $12/\sqrt n=1$ gives $n=144$.
Increasing the sample size does not automatically change the selection mechanism.
exam.answer: $144$; selection bias is not automatically removed.

exam.problem: A normal sample has $n=9,\bar x=12,s=3$, and $t_{0.975,8}=2.306$ is given. Calculate a mean interval and determine whether a two-sided test at the corresponding level rejects a population mean of ten.
exam.hint: Use the same model for the interval and test.
solution: The standard error is one, giving interval $[9.694,14.306]$.
Ten lies inside the interval.
exam.answer: Interval approximately $[9.694,14.306]$; do not reject a population mean of ten.

exam.problem: Four tosses of a fair coin are all heads. What is the $p$-value for a prespecified two-sided, probability-ordering exact binomial test? Why is it not the probability that the coin is fair?
exam.hint: Include the opposite tail with equally small probability mass under the null.
solution: Zero heads and four heads each have mass $1/16$; the other outcomes have larger mass.
Their sum is $1/8$.
The $p$-value assigns probabilities to outcomes under the null hypothesis; it does not specify a prior for the parameter.
exam.answer: $0.125$; it is not the posterior probability of the null hypothesis.

exam.problem: Three groups each contain three observations. Their means are two, four, and six, and each sample variance is one. Find the ANOVA $F$ statistic and degrees of freedom. Does rejection imply that every pair of group means differs?
exam.hint: Recover the within-group sum of squares from the summaries.
solution: The grand mean is four and the between-group sum of squares is twenty-four.
Each group's within-group sum of squares is two, for a total of six.
The ratio of mean squares is twelve, with degrees of freedom $(2,6)$. An overall rejection does not identify individual pairs.
exam.answer: $F=12$ with degrees of freedom $(2,6)$; it does not establish a difference for every pair.

exam.problem: The prior is $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$, and the data contain three successes and one failure. Give the posterior, predictive success probability, and at least four types of information to retain in an analysis report.
exam.hint: Retain more than a point estimate after updating.
solution: The posterior is $\operatorname{Beta}(4,2)$ and the predictive success probability is $2/3$.
Retain the observations and sampling design, prior and likelihood, effects and intervals, and diagnostics and limitations.
exam.answer: $\operatorname{Beta}(4,2)$ and $2/3$; report the design, model, precision, and limitations.

appendices.title: Prerequisites and Scope
appendices.text: The first four chapters require elementary algebra and summation. Continuous densities and transformations require single-variable integration; joint densities use basic double integrals, with links to the calculus volumes for review. This book covers a complete introductory undergraduate probability and statistics course. It does not develop measure theory, a full theory of stochastic processes, multiple regression, comprehensive experimental design, or advanced nonparametric inference. Poisson processes appear only as introductory context for count and waiting-time models.

appendices.title: Conditions for Expectation, Variance, and Convergence
appendices.text: Finite discrete supports allow direct summation; infinite supports require checking absolute integrability or the conditions for nonnegative integrals. The weak law of large numbers is proved using Chebyshev's inequality under finite variance. The classical CLT is stated and explored through simulations; a general proof requires characteristic functions or other probability tools. Finite simulations are not presented as proofs. The strong law and limit theory for dependent samples are not proved here.

appendices.title: Why Normal-Sample Variance Loses One Degree of Freedom
appendices.text: Decompose an independent standard-normal vector along the constant-vector direction and its orthogonal complement. The first projection determines the sample mean; the complement has dimension $n-1$, and its squared length gives a chi-square variable. Orthogonal components of a standard-normal vector are independent, yielding exact independence of the sample mean and sample variance. General nonnormal samples retain some moment identities but not this independence.

appendices.title: $t$, Chi-Square, $F$, and Numerical Probabilities
appendices.text: A $t$ variable is a standard normal divided by the square root of an independent chi-square variable divided by its degrees of freedom. The ratio of two independent chi-square variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom, gives $F$. Demonstrations calculate cumulative probabilities and quantiles using Gamma, regularized incomplete Beta/Gamma functions, and bisection. Readouts are floating-point approximations; displayed digits do not imply measurement precision.

appendices.title: Discrete Tails and Endpoint Conventions
appendices.text: Geometric and negative binomial variables in this book count the total trials, including the final success. Binomial right tails include the observed count. A probability-ordering two-sided binomial test sums outcomes whose null mass is no greater than the observed mass; this is not always twice a one-sided tail. Continuity corrections apply only to specified approximations, not to exact count probabilities.

appendices.title: Limits of Resampling and Permutation Methods
appendices.text: The ordinary bootstrap draws with replacement from the empirical distribution and preserves the original sample size. Percentile endpoints use linearly interpolated order-statistic quantiles; nominal coverage is not guaranteed for arbitrary small samples. The permutation demonstration enumerates all six equally likely assignments of four fixed outcomes to two groups of two. Exactness relies on randomization under a sharp null or on exchangeability. Bootstrap and permutation procedures are not interchangeable.

appendices.title: Confidence, Credibility, and Significance
appendices.text: Confidence-interval coverage is a repeated-sampling property of an interval procedure. A Bayesian credible interval describes parameter probability conditional on a prior, model, and data. A $p$-value evaluates extremeness under the null; it is not a parameter posterior. Statistical significance does not establish practical importance, causation, or model correctness. Multiple comparisons and stopping rules must be included in the full analysis procedure.

appendices.title: Writing a Reproducible Analysis
appendices.text: Retain raw data and units, missing-data handling, sampling or randomization design, prespecified questions and contrast directions, model assumptions, calculations, effects and uncertainty, diagnostics, sensitivity checks, and unverified assumptions. Label questions formed after exploration as exploratory rather than presenting them as prespecified tests. All simulations use visible, fixed seeds; changing a seed changes the finite sample, not the theoretical model.

body.text: Sample variance divides squared deviations from the sample mean by the degrees of freedom. Standard deviation has the original data's units.

body.title: Track units
body.text: Translation changes location but not spread. Scaling multiplies standard deviation by the absolute factor and variance by its square. This book computes quartiles by splitting about the median, excluding the overall median for odd sample sizes and taking each half's median.

formalDefinition.text: Sample variance requires $n\ge2$. A descriptive population variance may divide by the full count; state the convention.
conditions: Sample variance requires $n\ge2$. A descriptive population variance may divide by the full count; state the convention.

body.text: Once $B$ is known, retain only outcomes in $B$. The original intersection is the target event in this restricted space.

conditions: The conditioning event satisfies $P(B)>0$.

derivation.text: Retain the conditioning event.

body.title: Choose $z$ or $t$

body.title: Interpret coverage correctly
body.text: Before sampling, a random interval covers the fixed parameter with a specified probability. After observation the interval is fixed; frequentist confidence is not a posterior probability for the parameter.

formalDefinition.text: An exact $t$ interval requires independent normal observations and $n\ge2$.

body.title: Independent groups
body.text: Welch's method estimates each group's variance separately without imposing equality. Add the variances of the two means to obtain the squared standard error.

body.title: Approximate degrees of freedom

body.title: Paired data
body.text: Form independent paired differences, then apply a one-sample $t$ interval to them. The effective sample size is the number of pairs, not the total record count.

formalDefinition.text: The independent two-sample Welch interval is a standard approximation; small samples need an assessment of within-group normality.
conditions: The independent two-sample Welch interval is a standard approximation; small samples need an assessment of within-group normality.

lessons.title: Null hypotheses, $p$-values, and Type I errors
lessons.subtitle: A $p$-value measures how unusual the data are under the specified null model.
lessons.concept: A $p$-value measures how unusual the data are under the specified null model.
lessons.intuition: It asks what happens if we sample from this model, not directly how likely the hypothesis is to be true.

body.title: Prespecify the comparison
body.text: Specify the null, alternative direction, statistic, and significance level before seeing data. Do not choose the more favorable tail afterward.

body.title: Define the $p$-value
body.text: Under the null model, find the probability of statistics at least as supportive of the alternative as the observed value. The meaning of extreme depends on a prespecified ordering.

body.title: Distinguish errors
body.text: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis. Significance level controls a procedure's error probability; it is not the posterior probability that this particular conclusion is wrong.

formalDefinition.text: Specify the statistic and tails before observation, and justify the null distribution.

body.text: A two-sided alternative concerns both increases and decreases. For a symmetric $t$ distribution, use the absolute statistic to find both tails.

body.text: Under random assignment and the sharp null of zero treatment effect for every individual, reassign groups according to the design. Observational data require extra exchangeability assumptions.

lessons.title: Power, effect size, and multiple comparisons
lessons.subtitle: Detection probability depends on the true effect, noise, sample size, and decision threshold.
lessons.concept: Detection probability depends on the true effect, noise, sample size, and decision threshold.
lessons.intuition: Larger samples can make tiny effects statistically significant, so report practical magnitude too.

body.title: Separate errors from power
body.text: Type I error is defined under a true null. Type II error is defined under a specific alternative. Power is the probability of correctly rejecting under that alternative.

body.title: Specify the design objective
body.text: Power calculations need a meaningful target effect and scale. Post-hoc observed power based on the same estimated effect usually adds no substitute for interval information.

body.title: Control multiple opportunities
body.text: Testing many hypotheses creates more chances for false positives. Bonferroni uses the union bound to control familywise error under any dependence, though it can be conservative. Repeated looking and selection also need treatment.

formalDefinition.text: Power refers to a specified alternative parameter and test rule.
conditions: Power refers to a specified alternative parameter and test rule.
If every Bonferroni test has level at most $\alpha/m$, familywise error is at most $\alpha$.

derivation.text: Set the rejection region under the null.
Under the specified alternative, calculate probability of the same region.
For multiple tests, use the union bound to limit any false rejection.

practice.answer: The original error level is not guaranteed.

lessons.title: Contingency tables and chi-square tests
lessons.subtitle: Are observed category counts far enough from the counts expected under independence?
lessons.concept: Are observed category counts far enough from the counts expected under independence?
lessons.intuition: Use marginal proportions to predict each cell's count, then accumulate standardized squared deviations.

body.title: Calculate expected counts
body.text: The contingency-table null asserts row and column independence. Using observed margins, expected count is row total times column total divided by the grand total.

body.title: Measure deviation
body.text: Add squared cell deviations divided by expected counts. This measures departure from the null model. Row and column sum constraints determine degrees of freedom.

body.title: Check approximation conditions
body.text: Observational units must be independent and expected counts sufficiently large. This volume uses the conservative classroom rule of at least five in every cell. Sparse tables need exact or design-appropriate alternatives.

formalDefinition.text: This is a contingency-table independence test. Categories for each margin must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
conditions: This is a contingency-table independence test. Categories for each margin must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
Goodness-of-fit degrees of freedom instead equal category count minus one minus estimated parameter count. Do not interchange them.
Units must be independent, $N>0$, and all retained row and column margins positive. Remove impossible empty categories before calculating degrees of freedom.

Chi-square tail probabilities are asymptotic approximations. This volume uses at least five expected observations per cell as a conservative classroom rule; sparse tables need another suitable method.

derivation.text: Under independence, a joint proportion is the product of its marginals.
Multiply by the grand total to obtain expected counts.
Accumulate scaled deviations and use the asymptotic chi-square reference.

body.title: Separate fitting from modeling
body.text: Least squares is a calculation on fixed data. Statistical inference additionally needs assumptions about the linear response mean and error behavior.

body.title: Calculate slope and intercept
body.text: Divide joint variation by squared input variation for the slope. The intercept makes the fitted line pass through the sample center.

body.title: Inspect residuals
body.text: A residual is observed minus fitted response, not perpendicular geometric distance to the line. Curvature, funnels, or time patterns can reveal omitted structure.

formalDefinition.text: Simple least squares with an intercept requires $S_{xx}>0$.
conditions: Simple least squares with an intercept requires $S_{xx}>0$.

lessons.concept: Estimating an average response is easier than predicting a new observation.

body.title: State the error model
body.text: Classical exact inference treats inputs as fixed and errors as independent normal variables with zero mean and common variance. Residual plots can diagnose problems but cannot prove these assumptions.

body.title: Estimate the slope's scale
body.text: Divide residual sum of squares by sample size minus two to estimate common error variance: slope and intercept were both fitted.

body.title: Distinguish the two intervals
body.text: A mean-response interval includes uncertainty in estimating the mean. A prediction interval adds one new error variance. Both widen away from the mean input.

formalDefinition.text: Exact $t$ inference requires the stated linear model with independent homoscedastic normal errors and $n>2$.
conditions: Exact $t$ inference requires the stated linear model with independent homoscedastic normal errors and $n>2$.
For a prediction interval, add one inside the square root. The new error must be independent and follow the same model.

body.title: Decompose sums of squares
body.text: Split total variation into between-group and within-group sums of squares. Weight between-group contributions by group sample sizes.

body.title: Compare per degree of freedom
body.text: Divide each sum by its degrees of freedom to obtain a mean square. Under independent homoscedastic normal errors and equal null means, their ratio has an $F$ distribution.

body.title: Interpret the overall rejection
body.text: Rejection means not all means agree; it does not imply every pair differs. Plan follow-up comparisons or control multiplicity. Unequal variances may require an adapted method.

formalDefinition.text: Classical exact one-way ANOVA requires independence, normality within groups, and a common variance.
conditions: Classical exact one-way ANOVA requires independence, normality within groups, and a common variance.
Require $k\ge2,N>k$ and positive within-group mean square. Zero noise needs separate treatment.

derivation.text: Split every deviation into within-group and between-group parts.
Within-group deviations sum to zero, canceling the cross terms.
Divide by the respective degrees of freedom and take the ratio under the null.

lessons.title: Beta–binomial updating and a complete analysis report
lessons.subtitle: Bayesian inference combines a prior and likelihood into a posterior parameter distribution.
lessons.concept: Bayesian inference combines a prior and likelihood into a posterior parameter distribution.
lessons.intuition: It allows probability statements about parameters within a specified model; conclusions therefore depend on both prior and likelihood.

body.title: Specify a prior
body.text: A Beta density describes uncertainty about success probability between zero and one. Two positive shape parameters control location and concentration. They are not unconditionally literal historical success and failure counts.

body.title: Update the posterior
body.text: For independent Bernoulli trials, add success and failure exponents to the prior. The posterior mean combines prior and sample information and equals the posterior predictive success probability.

body.title: Write a complete report
body.text: State the question, observational units, sampling or assignment design, model assumptions, effect and interval, diagnostics, and limitations. A credible interval is a posterior probability statement conditional on prior, model, and data; do not conflate it with frequentist confidence.

formalDefinition.text: Prior shape parameters satisfy $a,b>0$. The likelihood assumes a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with a common probability.
conditions: Prior shape parameters satisfy $a,b>0$. The likelihood assumes a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with a common probability.
Posterior and prediction depend on the specified model. Do not hide prior sensitivity behind a point estimate.

derivation.text: Write the parameter-dependent part of the prior density.
Multiply by the binomial likelihood.
Recognize the normalized Beta distribution and calculate its mean.

workedExamples.title: Update a uniform prior

workedExamples.answer: The posterior predictive success probability is $8/12=2/3$.

practice.hint: Add successes and failures to the corresponding shapes.

practice.problem: Success probability has posterior $\operatorname{Beta}(3,6)$. Find the posterior predictive probability of success in the next Bernoulli trial.
practice.hint: Divide the first shape by the sum of shapes.

practice.problem: Does a posterior $95\%$ credible interval mean the same thing as a frequentist $95\%$ confidence interval?
practice.hint: Parameter probability and repeated-sampling coverage differ.
solution: The first uses the prior-updated parameter distribution; the second describes an interval-generating procedure.

commonMistakes.correction: Posterior probability and repeated-sampling coverage are different statements.
